title: Draft: Linux (eBPF): capture process information of packets.
description:
Captures process information related to packets using BPF CO-RE (Compile once, Run everywhere) functionality. I began by writing a bpf program with 8 kprobes that are compiled when running cmake. (Cmake might require you to install the latest clang and llvm) . The kprobes are then conditionally attached to their respective kernel functions, if, when the user selects start capture, he has selected a new process information column under **edit -\> preferences -\> columns.** 

This column shows the pid, comm, parent pid, parent comm, grandparent pid and grandparent comm for the displayed packet if one of the 8 kernel functions from ebpf_packet_capture.c was used by the process that sent or received that packet. For enabling this conditional loading of the kprobes I had to modify the dumpcap commandline args before wireshark spawns it to have an additional "--process-info" argument. Which, if present, the kprobes are loaded and wireshark captures process information and then unattaches them when dumpcap ends ( I have to review the code of unattaching the probes and whether it works correctly.).

partially Fixes #1184

I have used the pcapng's enhanced packet block's options functionality to pass a process_info struct that contains all the aforementioned process information. The process information is passed based on whether the pid is 0 or not, 0 is the default value for the pid which means that no information for that packet's process was captured. 

The information for the packets' processes is stored in bpf maps, hash maps that are available to use in bpf programs. Each packet's process information struct is stored against a port key that comprises off the source and the destination port, the source port is in host byte order and destination in network byte in the kernel whereas both are in network byte order in userspace so we convert any port in network order to host byte order and then construct the port key. in the kernel space the process information is captured and stored against the port key for every packet that passes through the functions and in userspace in dumpcap we query the map with port keys from dumpcap for every packet captured.

Further based on whether the process information is available or not (pid is 0 or not (pid is set to 0 for each packet before checking whether info is present in bpf maps.)) we add an option in pcapng_write_enhanced_packet_block to write the option for the process information struct and then while parsing the options in pcapng_read we parse our custom option as well. after first initializing a process_info struct we store the passed information in options to a modified wtap_rec's process_info struct. and that information is then available in packet_info \*pinfo's wtap_rec structure in the dissectors where in the packet-frame.c dissect_frame() function we conditionally set the value of the process info column to a neatly formatted process info struct's values or to an empty string.

Attached file of example process information captured. The first 6 packets process information was not captured. While the remaining packets process information was. 
This was because the process that initiated the conversation for the first 6 packets used a non traditional kernal method to send those packets. This is an area that we still have to account for with the current implementation. But with CAP_SYS_ADMIN this should be pretty easy to implement without any performance impact.

Maybe it was premature to add the merge request Jaap. But I'm working on clearing as many issues as I can. Thanks for your input. But it could've been better if you could have provided some instances for some of the above as I'm trying to search for precompile statements that shouldn't be there and I'm yet to remove and other issues like the ones you mentioned.

But I have a query about the implementation - which works quite well on my linux machine, Jaap, I assure you, and should work well on any linux machine given my bpf code is CO-RE compliant. And I do feel that it would be a great addition to wireshark. I haven't used wireshark in security critical environments but only as a learning tool but I always thought that it was missing this one really interesting option.

Anyways I'm faced with a critical implementation decision.

It seems that CAP_SYS_ADMIN is a prerequisite for attaching kprobes.

So I could either implement the current functionality using tracepoints which are slower and work with CAP_BPF which will need to be enabled.

Or I can stick to kprobes that work really well. But they require dumpcap to run with CAP_SYS_ADMIN (At least till the kprobes are attached. Maybe not after that, But I'm not sure.)

So what should I do.

In the meanwhile I'll keep at cleaning the code.

Also I ran `git diff --check` but it seems not to list the whitespace errors. Does it automatically correct them? Not sure but the pipeline doesn't show trailing whitespaces errors on running git diff --check.

So this is going to require us to force users to set CAP_SYS_ADMIN on dumpcap.
That besides the already required CAP_NET_RAW and CAP_NET_ADMIN.
This needs some serious consideration.
Or we can go with tracepoints. That works with CAP_BPF but is slower. However when we implement it for windows I think we'll need admin then.

Also the CAP_SYS_ADMIN privilege is only retained if the process information column is selected by the user.

We could notify the user that dumpcap will run as admin in such a scenario, so it stays upto them whether they want to enable it or not. That way they'll have the ability to choose to use the feature or not and we aren't hiding anything from them. Although I don't know how user friendly such information is. We could say it more colloquially - like selecting process information will make dumpcap run more vulnerably, as an example.

And since CAP_SYS_ADMIN is enabled we could also modify the code to display all processes associated with the socket instead of just the one that sent the packet and it's parent and grandparent.

I had limited myself to that as I thought we would run with CAP_BPF, not knowing CAP_SYS_ADMIN was required at the time. 

But with CAP_SYS_ADMIN we could loop through the proc/[pid] directories once at the start and capture all the socket's and their associated pids.

After that we could hook kprobes to when the connections are created and associate the new processes that create sockets that way which is much faster than userspace looping and we shouldn't miss any process if we hook to the right functions.
